body:
`unflatten()` takes quadratic time in the number of reference tokens of one key on current `develop` (3.13.0 work in progress; 3.12.0 is linear). An object with one key of 100,000 `/0` tokens (200 KB) takes 2.4 s; 3.12.0 needs 5 ms. The time quadruples with each doubling of the key. An attacker who controls one key of an object passed to `unflatten()` can make the process busy for minutes with a few megabytes of input. `unflatten.md` promises "Linear in the size of the JSON value".

## Cause

3.13.0 decides in a first pass which prefixes of the keys denote arrays (those that have a reference token `0` among their children), so that the result no longer depends on the order of the keys, and looks the prefixes up again in the second pass. A prefix was identified by hashing it and by comparing it byte by byte with the set entry, from its beginning, so a key with n tokens cost n²/2 bytes. For `ordered_json` (and any unsorted object type) the shortcut for keys that share a beginning with the previous key does not help: four keys were enough to be quadratic.

## Change

- Prefixes shorter than 64 bytes stay in the hash table and are compared as before (a bounded number of bytes).
- Longer prefixes are kept in a tree whose nodes are looked up by their parent and the text of one token. The node of a prefix is found by walking the tokens of the key from the root, so all prefixes of a key together cost one pass over the key and no prefix is compared as a whole. The nodes along the key walked last are kept, so keys with a common beginning do not walk it again. No recursion.
- The hash function is seeded with a value derived from the address of a local variable (ASLR changes it between processes). With the previous fixed constants, crafted keys could be made to collide: 20,000 keys of 18 bytes with equal hash took 0.5 s instead of 7 ms. Where addresses are not randomized, or if the seed is known, k short prefixes (< 64 bytes) can still collide and cost k²/2 comparisons of fewer than 64 bytes. Results never depend on the seed.
- The array/object decision and the independence from the key order are unchanged. Only private helpers of `detail::json_pointer` changed.

## Measurements (Apple clang -O2, arm64)

`unflatten()` of one key with n tokens `/0`:

| | n=25k | n=50k | n=100k | n=200k |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 175 ms | 617 ms | 2437 ms | 9729 ms |
| after | 4 ms | 6 ms | 12 ms | 27 ms |
| 3.12.0 | 1 ms | 3 ms | 5 ms | 10 ms |

`ordered_json`, 4 keys (`/0`×m `/a0`, `/10`, `/0`×m `/a1`, `/11`): before 397 / 1402 / 5191 / 20723 ms for m = 25k / 50k / 100k / 200k, after 4 / 7 / 15 / 33 ms, 3.12.0 2 / 3 / 8 / 17 ms.

Ordinary documents (`flatten()` then `unflatten()`, instructions retired): within 0.3 % of before for canada, citm_catalog, twitter, jeopardy, mesh, update-center and random. A realistic deep document (100 levels, 100k leaves): +1.5 % instructions, +5-12 % wall time vs `develop`, and about 9× faster than 3.12.0.

**Known trade-off:** two thousand different long keys (2000 keys × 2000 unique tokens, 12 MB of keys) take 1.4 s instead of 3.1 s on `develop`, but still about 6× longer than 3.12.0 (0.2 s) and use about 300 MiB more memory for the tree (about 78 bytes per token). 3.13.0 needs a set entry per prefix for the order independence anyway; path compression of unique tails would reduce this further and is left for a follow-up.

## Tests

`unit-json_pointer.cpp`: semantics of the array/object decision (prefixes around the 64-byte hand-over, different token splits of one prefix, escapes, tokens longer than a word), a random round trip in shuffled key order with `ordered_json`, and a time-ratio check (best of 3 CPU-time runs, the same keys with an array-hitting token vs. token `a`; seven shapes including the 4-key `ordered_json` shape; ratio about 3 now, 25 to 300 on the previous code, bound 6 or 10). The test fails on `develop` and on the intermediate version that still had the `ordered_json` problem. It was run 50× 8 in parallel and 64× 16 in parallel at -O0 and -O1 without a failure.

Differential tests against `develop` (about 150,000 randomized flattened objects, `json` and shuffled `ordered_json`, with `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS`) gave identical results and error messages. Allocation failure was injected at every allocation of one `unflatten()` call: no leaks. The suite passes under ASan and UBSan; clang-tidy 22, clang `-Weverything` and g++ 16 report nothing new.

## Also: a key that is a prefix of an earlier key (#6105)

This PR also fixes #6105, which is in the same function. With an object type that keeps the insertion order (`ordered_json`), a key such as `/a` can come after `/a/b`. The final assignment then replaced the object built for `/a/b` without an error: `{"/a/b":2,"/a":1}` gave `{"a":1}`, `{"/a/0/b":1,"/a/0":2}` gave `{"a":[2]}` and `{"/x":1,"":2}` gave `2`. `json` never sees this, because `std::map` visits the shorter key first and the walk of the longer key throws `type_error.313`. 3.12.0 has the same bug.

`unflatten()` now throws `type_error.313` when the target of the final assignment is no longer null, so the result no longer depends on the key order. A `null` value keeps the container, as it does for `json` when the shorter key comes first: `{"/a/b":2,"/a":null}` gives `{"a":{"b":2}}` for both object types. This case is not exotic, because `flatten()` turns empty objects and arrays into `null`.

The branch is not reached for `json` or any sorted object type. `continue` skips only the assignment, so the cached prefix nodes stay valid. Tests in `unit-json_pointer.cpp` cover the three inputs above, the reverse order, and the `null` cases for `json` and `ordered_json`; 5 of the new assertions fail without the change. `unflatten.md` documents the new `type_error.313` case and has a version-history note.

Fixes #6105.

## Breaking changes

No breaking changes to the API. The speed-up changes only private helpers. With an object type that keeps the insertion order, an input with a key that is a prefix of an earlier key now throws the documented `type_error.313` instead of silently dropping data (bug fix, #6105); `json` behaves as before.
